To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 20 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .01 For three of five traits, we observed a statistical difference between predictions using words shared with the mirror AI and those shared with the inverse AI-Neuroticism (r = .60 vs r = -.25: t(92) = 8.49, p < .001), Extraversion (r = .44 vs r = .04: t(92) = 3.78, p < .01), and Openness (r = .45 vs r = .15: t(92) = 2.96, p < .05).
p < .05 For three of five traits, we observed a statistical difference between predictions using words shared with the mirror AI and those shared with the inverse AI-Neuroticism (r = .60 vs r = -.25: t(92) = 8.49, p < .001), Extraversion (r = .44 vs r = .04: t(92) = 3.78, p < .01), and Openness (r = .45 vs r = .15: t(92) = 2.96, p < .05).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 5 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .134 Providing the rater with the full participant-AI conversation versus what participants wrote versus only the content words and pronouns participants wrote did not reliably change the rater’s prediction (F(1.45, 141.85) = 2.16, p = .134, ηp² = .02).
p = .19 There was no difference in the number of words they produced with each (t(94) = -1.31, p = .19, dz = -.13).
p = .17 As in Experiment 1, the highest correlation was observed for Neuroticism (r(93) = .63, 95% CI [.49, .74], p < .001) and the lowest for Conscientiousness (r(93) = .14, 95% CI [-.06, .33], p = .17).
p = .25 There was no difference in the number of these words participants wrote with each (t(94) = -1.15, p = .25, dz = -.12).
p = .14 Applying this filter left a median of 180 participant words (range: 65 to 540) with the mirror AI and 197 participant words (range: 54 to 543) with the inverse AI, with no statistical difference in word counts between these conditions (t(94) = -1.51, p = .14, dz = -.16).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 3 distinct packages/libraries: httr2, jsonlite, readxl. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 192 columns across 8 data files.

Issues Identified

21 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.

In a preregistered study, 100 participants completed the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI) and then engaged in unstructured, text-based conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.

In Castiello et al. (2026) https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/redj/?noauthor=1 100 participants completed the BFI and then had conversations with two versions of GPT-4.1-one instructed to mirror their personality through language, and the other instructed to present the inverse (or opposite) of their personality.

We recruited 200 participants from Prolific-100 for Experiment 1 and 100 for Experiment 2.

Participants were native English speakers aged 18 to 50 from Canada, the US, and the UK.

Participants were excluded if they failed to complete the study, failed an attention check embedded in the questionnaire, or wrote fewer than 130 words during the LLM interaction.

Participants were compensated for their time at £10/hour (Experiment 1) and £7/hour (Experiment 2).

Participants completed the experiment on their own computer.

Participants completed the 44-item version of the Big Five Inventory (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/AwJp/?prefix=BFI%3B John et al., 2012).

Participants had unstructured, text-based conversations with GPT-4.1 (OpenAI) instructed to mimic a specific BFI trait profile through language.

Following completion of the consent form, participants completed the BFI-44 (John et al., 2012).

Participants were blind to the length of the interaction.

Ninety-nine participants completed the BFI questionnaire, and then had an unstructured chat with the LLM GPT-4.1.

Using a similar method to Experiment 1, 95 participants completed the BFI, and then had an unstructured chat with two LLMs.

Participants had conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words.

For example, Lucas et al., (2014) demonstrated that participants were willing to disclose more personal information to a virtual human when they believed it was being controlled by a computer versus a person.

For Experiment 1, the values were based on mean BFI trait scores (rounded to the nearest half digit) from Prolific participants in Castiello et al. (2026): Openness: 3.5; Conscientiousness: 4; Extraversion: 3; Agreeableness: 4; and Neuroticism: 2.5.

Ethics approval statement:

The University of Oxford Central University Research Ethics Committee (CUREC; R86261/RE001) and the Acadia University Research Ethics Committee approved this study.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

id sample_size
fy569f We will collect data from 100 participants via Prolific. Participants will be native English speakers recruited from the UK, the US, and Canada. The sample size is based on a pilot study where we observed statistically significant correlations between self-report BFI scores, and LLM (Claude)-predicted BFI scores, with 50 people.
Field Preregistration 1
template_name AsPredicted
id fy569f
link https://aspredicted.org/fy569f.pdf
title BFI LLM Prediction Study - Summer 2026
date_created 2026/07/03 10:09 (PT)
date_registered 2026-07-03
existing_data_explanation No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
research_questions Our study seeks to address the question, can large-language models (LLMs) such as Anthropic’s Claude predict people’s Big Five Inventory (BFI) personality profiles from a brief (~ 500 word) text-based interaction with an LLM? We predict that there will be positive, statistically significant correlations between the personality traits generated by Claude and participants’ actual Big Five Inventory (BFI) scores for each big five trait: extraversion, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness, and agreeableness.
design_dependent_variables The dependent variable is the Pearson correlation coefficients between Claude’s predicted Big Five trait scores and participants’ self-reported scores.
study_design_overview This correlational study has a single condition. Participants will complete the 44-item version of the Big Five Inventory (John, Donahue & Kentle, 1991). They will then have an unstructured, text-based interaction with GPT 4.1 requiring 26 turns. Participants will be instructed to get to know the AI, interacting with it as they would a new friend. Following the interaction, participants will complete a post chat Questionnaire (Castiello et al., 2026) to assess the extent to which they connected with the AI.
statistical_tests Participant’s trait scores from their completed BFI-44 questionnaire, as well as the transcript from their text-based LLM interaction will be collected for analyses. Their transcripts will be given to Claude Sonnet 4.6. Claude will be prompted to assess each participant’s personality profile, focusing solely on what the participant said during the interaction (i.e. vocabulary choices, topics discussed, emotional tones and interpersonal styles). Claude will then be asked to complete the BFI-44 questionnaire as if it were the participant. Mean scores for each of the five BFI traits will be subsequently calculated from Claude’s responses.

We will conduct a correlation analysis between Claude’s predicted scores and participants’ self-reported scores for each of the five BFI-44 traits. We will control for multiple comparisons by applying a Holm-Bonferroni correction. Statistical significance will be assessed using corrected p-values at an alpha level of 0.05. We will also calculate the root-mean-square error (RMSE) between the predicted and actual scores for each trait.
outliers_and_exclusions Participants who fail the attention checks in our study’s questionnaires, as well as those who do not complete the entirety of the study (both the questionnaires and the AI chatbot interaction), will be excluded from further analyses. Participants who write fewer than 130 words (less than 5 words per turn) in their interaction with the LLM will be excluded from further analyses.
sample_size We will collect data from 100 participants via Prolific. Participants will be native English speakers recruited from the UK, the US, and Canada. The sample size is based on a pilot study where we observed statistically significant correlations between self-report BFI scores, and LLM (Claude)-predicted BFI scores, with 50 people.
additional_comments We predict that the strength of the correlations between LLM-predicted and actual BFI trait scores will depend on the number of messages from each participant that Claude is given. As the number of participant messages used in the prediction decreases from 26 messages to 13 to 5, the average correlation across each of the five BFI traits will decrease.

The prompt used by Claude to predict BFI scores is posted here: https://github.com/drlametti/bfi_prediction_study
paper_id input

A statistical difference was still observed for predictions of Neuroticism between the mirror and inverse conditions (r = .49 vs r = -.07: t(92) = 5.26, p < .001). r = .49; r = -.07 t(92) = 5.26 t-test indeterminate none No parseable d effect size found. NA NA NA
