How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

:::

Full text

Abstract

Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI). In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI as if it were each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats. Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members. A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater's predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax. Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI's persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation. A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1-one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI). The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report. Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, and dropped to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone. People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI's persona mirrors the users.

Every week, more than a billion people have conversations with AI systems like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Here we investigate the extent to which the words we choose to use in human-AI interactions convey our personality traits. We show that personality traits can be predicted from only a few hundred words of unstructured conversation with AI, and this is enhanced if the AI's persona mirrors the person's personality-a phenomenon that may occur in both human-to-human and human-AI interactions. The findings imply that people are sharing a great deal of their psychological profile with technology companies in even short interactions with language-based AI systems.

Introduction

More than a billion people talk with large language models (LLMs) every week (OpenAI, 2026). In addition to communicating commands and questions, the words we choose to say in these interactions may reveal meaningful information about our psychology (Mairesse et al., 2007; Rude et al., 2004 https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/11Li+Yxak. There's precedent for the idea that we convey more than just the plain meaning of our prose in online writing. Personality, gender, and age are recoverable from the text of social media posts, although these predictions require thousands of words (Schwartz et al., 2013). How much information do we convey about our personality in conversations with AI? And to what extent does the persona of the AI shape what we transmit? Here, in a preregistered experiment and a second study involving the reanalysis of published data, we address these questions by testing whether Big Five personality traits can be predicted from short, unstructured chats with AI.

The Big Five model is a trait taxonomy of human personality with five dimensions-openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (OCEAN). The model has its roots in the lexical hypothesis of human personality-or the idea that the important psychological traits that differentiate people are reflected in natural language (e.g., Dan is studious, while Robin is lazy) (Galton, 1884; John et al., 1988). Consistent with this, the five traits were first observed in clusters of words that people use to describe each other (Costa & McCrae, 1992; Goldberg, 1981 Goldberg, , 1990 Goldberg, , 1993;; John et al., 2012; John & Srivastava, 1999; Norman, 1963; Tupes & Christal, 1992). Commonly measured using self-report questionnaires (John et al.https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/AwJp 2012) , the Big Five have been observed across cultures and in different stages of human development (Bleidorn et al., 2018 (Bleidorn et al., , 2022;; McCrae & Costa, 1997; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000). Self-ratings have high test-retest reliability (Gnambs, 2014; John & Srivastava, 1999) and show self-other agreement with ratings made by friends and family, suggesting that these questionnaires capture traits that others can see (Ashton & Lee, 2025; Connelly & Ones, 2010).

Since the development of the Big Five, a body of work has examined the external validity of the traits and if they have a genetic basis. The five factors predict life outcomes such as school grades (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/7czom. Chen et al.https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/7czom 2025) https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/DFvbK job performance (Zell & Lesickhttps://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/5tyR+jEL1+JqC2+kbop 2022) , antisocial behaviour (Corff & Toupin, 2009; John et al., 1994; Jolliffe, 2013; Jones et al., 2011) , and some psychological disorders (Kang et al., 2024; Kotov et al., 2010). Neuroticism, in particular, is strongly associated with disorders of mental health like anxiety and depression (Jeronimus et al., 2016; Kotov et al., 2010). Twin studies suggest that the traits have a genetic basis (Jang et al.https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/JbORr+kDMFg+tVzEO 1996; Lo et al., 2017; Vukasović & Bratko, 2015) , with evidence that the factors are linked to a distinct set of common genetic variants (Schwaba et al., 2026). Taken together, research on the external validity of the Big Five suggests that the factors reflect behaviourally relevant dimensions of our psychology that are shaped by the environment, our genes, and reflected in the language people use (Byrom & Murphy, 2018).

The Big Five are typically measured using self-report questionnaires, but social expectations and demand characteristics can bias these measures (Paulhus, 1984; Vazire, 2010). To address these problems, researchers have attempted to measure personality using the language that people choose to speak or write in naturalistic contexts (Hirsh & Peterson, 2009; Mairesse et al., 2007; Pennebaker & King, 1999; Yarkoni, 2010). These approaches use conventional linguistic analyses, and, increasingly, machine learning, to exploit associations between the words people use and their personality traits (Pennebaker et al., 2003; Schwartz et al., 2013 https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/kfYP+5NhT. Extraverts, for example, tend to write words like bar and dancing in blog posts, while introverts use words like cats and computer (Yarkoni, 2010). Bespoke software-based analyses of natural language can generate personality profiles that correlate with self-report questionnaires in the range of r = .2 to .4 (Mairesse et al., 2007; Park et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 2013). But LLMs like GPT and Claude-trained to produce language based on learned associations in vast amounts of online text (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/KzRd. Brown et al., 2020)-now match or, in some cases, outperform custom software-based approaches (Peters & Matz, 2024).

In recent work, Wright et al. (2026) compared predictions of personality traits from seven different LLMs. The predictions were based on personal language generated by different groups: One group produced stream-of-consciousness thought for 30 minutes generating an average of 3,097 words per participant, while the other group recorded daily video journals over 2 to 3 weeks generating an average of 1,651 words per participant. When the prediction was based on stream of consciousness thought, correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported traits averaged r = .44; when it was based on journal entries, they averaged r = .57. For some traits, the correlations exceeded those between self-report and judgements made by family (Connelly & Ones, 2010). Thus, LLMs can detect meaningful signals of personality in a few pages of free-form personal language.

Although language is a tool for personal thought, its primary function is communication (Clark, 1996; Fedorenko et al., 2024). How much of our personality do we convey in short conversations? And, if personality seeps into these interactions, does the fidelity of the signal depend on the personality of our conversational partners? Here, we address these questions using LLMs, which people increasingly have conversations with.

In a preregistered study, 100 participants completed the 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI) and then engaged in unstructured, text-based conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. GPT-4.1 was instructed to act like a friend during the conversation, and to convey an average Big Five personality profile through language. A second LLM rater-Claude Sonnet 4.6-was then tasked with predicting each participant's Big Five profile based on the text of the conversation alone. We hypothesized that correlations between the rater's predicted traits scores and participants' self-reported scores, would be positive and significant for all Big Five traits. We also predicted that the strength of these correlations would depend on the proportion of the conversation the rater was given.

In a second experiment, we used data we collected previously to replicate and extend the results of Experiment 1. Both humans and LLMs come to mirror the word choice of conversational partners (Blevins, 2026; P. Chen et al., 2026; Garrod & Anderson, 1987). This phenomenon, known as convergence, is thought to aid communication-but it might also facilitate the communication of personality traits by promoting feelings of connection. People affiliate more with LLMs that mirror aspects of their personality through word choice and linguistic style in conversation (Castiello et al., 2026). In Castiello et al. (2026) https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/redj/?noauthor=1 100 participants completed the BFI and then had conversations with two versions of GPT-4.1-one instructed to mirror their personality through language, and the other instructed to present the inverse (or opposite) of their personality. In the present study, we had the LLM rater predict participants' personality traits based on the text of these conversations. These predictions were then correlated with participants' self-reported traits, and the correlations were compared between mirror and inverse AI chats. We hypothesized that correlations between the LLM rater's predicted traits scores and participants' self-reported trait scores, would be stronger when the rater's predictions were based on conversations with an LLM that mirrored personality.

Finally, in both experiments we tested the extent to which the LLM rater used lexical information, as opposed to syntax and conversational context, to predict personality traits. If personality is conveyed largely through the words people use, the LLM rater should be able to reliably predict participants' personality using only a list of content words and pronouns shared by participants in each conversation.

Methods

Transparency, Openness, and Data Availability

Experiment 1 was preregistered on July 3, 2026 (https://aspredicted.org/fy569f.pdf). Experiment 2 was not preregistered for this current hypothesis, but was preregistered for our previous study (Castiello, et al. 2026). Processed data from all experiments, LLM prompts, and the R script used for predicting BFI traits from conversations are available at https://github.com/drlametti/bfi_prediction_study. For ethical reasons, we cannot publicly share participant conversations with AI, but they are available upon reasonable request.

Participants

We recruited 200 participants from Prolific-100 for Experiment 1 and 100 for Experiment 2. We collected the Experiment 2 data before Experiment 1 as part of Castiello et al. (2026). Participants were native English speakers aged 18 to 50 from Canada, the US, and the UK. We based the sample size on correlations observed in a pilot study with 50 participants using the same methods. Participants were excluded if they failed to complete the study, failed an attention check embedded in the questionnaire, or wrote fewer than 130 words during the LLM interaction. Based on these criteria, we excluded six participants from the study, leaving a sample size of 99 in Experiment 1 and 95 in Experiment 2.

Participants' median age was 34; 95 identified as female, 103 identified as male, and 2 identified as nonbinary. Participants were compensated for their time at £10/hour (Experiment 1) and £7/hour (Experiment 2). The University of Oxford Central University Research Ethics Committee (CUREC; R86261/RE001) and the Acadia University Research Ethics Committee approved this study.

Software and Materials

Participants completed the experiment on their own computer. All interactions-e.g., the consent form, questionnaires, LLM chats, and the debriefing form-were designed, built, and delivered in a browser using the conversational AI software Generative Studio X (http://onereach.ai). We conducted the analyses and created the figures in RStudio (Posit PBC). The R scripts that generated a prediction of participants' personality traits via an API-based interaction with Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic) were written with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic). Claude Code was also used to draft R scripts that identified specific classes of words (e.g., content words) in human-AI conversations. To ensure accuracy, two of the study's authors independently audited these scripts for errors. Personality predictions also aligned with those made using the same prompt and data in https://claude.ai/ chat.

Questionnaires

Participants completed the 44-item version of the Big Five Inventory (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/AwJp/?prefix=BFI%3B John et al., 2012). This self-report questionnaire assessed individuals' trait scores across each of the Big Five personalities (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/AIfT/?prefix=Openness%2C%20Conscientiousness%2C%20Extraversion%2C%20Agreeableness%2C%20and%20Neuroticism%3B Costa & McCrae, 1992) using short statements. Participants indicated their level of agreement with each of the statements using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Language Model Prompts

Participants had unstructured, text-based conversations with GPT-4.1 (OpenAI) instructed to mimic a specific BFI trait profile through language. In Experiment 1, the LLM was prompted to convey a trait profile that reflected average BFI scores from a prior study that had a similar online sample (Castiello et al., 2026). In Experiment 2, we used participant BFI scores (measured prior to the interaction) to create bespoke GPT-4.1 personalities that either mirrored a participant's trait profile in conversation (mirror), or presented the opposite trait profile (inverse). Critically, all three prompts were identical with the exception of the numeric BFI trait scores GPT-4.1 was told to convey (see Appendix 1). GPT-4.1 was also instructed to communicate like someone chatting with a friend, using a mix of statements, reflections, and questions. The LLM started each conversation with, Hey, how are you? ; the LLM then generated responses based on its prompted personality, what the participant said, and all prior exchanges in the conversation.

In both experiments, we used Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic) as a rater to predict participant BFI trait scores based on their conversation with GPT-4.1. We chose to use this LLM as the rater over other options because in a recent study Sonnet successfully predicted personality traits based on longer personal narratives (Wright et al., 2026) and the model was inexpensive compared to newer models.

The rater was instructed to review the transcript of a GPT-participant interaction and, based on the conversation, generate a one sentence description outlining what the messages revealed about each of the participant's Big Five traits (see Appendix 1). For example, "Openness: The participant shows curiosity across diverse domains-cybersecurity, gaming simulators, travel, and psychology-shifting topics fluidly and engaging with new information eagerly, suggesting a broadly curious and exploratory intellectual style." In a second step, the rater was instructed to complete the BFI-44 as if it were the participant. We modelled this approach-instructing an LLM to complete a personality test mimicking a particular person-after Wright et al. (2026). We used modified versions of the prompt to have Sonnet 4.6 generate personality predictions based solely on the messages participants wrote or on an alphabetized list of the content words and pronouns they wrote (Appendix 1).

Procedure

Following completion of the consent form, participants completed the BFI-44 (John et al., 2012). In Experiment 1, participants then began to text with an LLM-GPT-4.1-named Alex. They were told the goal of the interaction was to converse with the LLM to determine if they would get along with it if it were a person; thus, participants knew they were chatting with an AI. In Experiment 2, the completion of the BFI-44 was followed by chats with two LLMs-one named Alex and the other named Pat. The instruction was the same as in Experiment 1. Unbeknownst to participants, one LLM reflected their BFI profile in its language and conversational style (mirror AI), while the other LLM reflected the opposite of their BFI trait profile in its language and conversational style (inverse AI). We counterbalanced the names of the LLMs (Alex and Pat) and order of interactions (mirror and inverse) across participants (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/redj/?prefix=see Castiello et al., 2026). In both experiments the chats required 26 conversational turns. Participants were blind to the length of the interaction. The top panel of Figure 1 shows the flow of tasks in each experiment.

Data Analyses

The LLM rater inferred answers to the BFI-44 10 times for each participant in independent runs. As there was some variability in the inference from run to run (the average SD across traits was .14 of a point on the 1 to 5 scale), we computed BFI trait scores for each of the 10 runs and then we found the average BFI trait scores across the runs. The primary preregistered hypothesis (Experiment 1) was that, based on text from an unstructured 26-turn interaction with an LLM, the rater could predict participants' BFI traits at greater than chance. To test this, we computed two-tailed Pearson correlations for each trait between the rater's inferred trait scores and participants' actual self-reported scores. Permutation tests-in which the correlation was computed 10,000 times based on a random pairing of predicted trait scores with actual trait scores-identified whether the target or experimentally observed Pearson correlation fell outside the permuted null distribution.

As a secondary preregistered hypothesis (Experiment 1), we predicted that the rater's ability to infer participants' BFI traits would decrease if the rater was given fewer than the total number of 26 conversational turns from each chat. To test this, we chose a random sample of 13 turns for each participant.

Based on this fixed selection, the LLM rater inferred answers to the BFI-44 10 times for each participant in independent runs. Trait scores were found for each run, and then averaged across the 10 runs. We then selected 5 random turns from the selection of 13 turns (that is, the 5 turns were nested within the 13), and the rater repeated the inference. We computed correlations for each trait between the rater-predicted trait scores with 13 and 5 conversational turns and participants' actual self-reported scores.

We also examined the extent to which the LLM rater's predictions of personality traits depended on conversational context and syntax versus lexical content alone. To do this, the rater generated predictions based on the text participants wrote without the conversational LLM's responses. We also had the rater generate predictions based solely on the nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs that each participant wrote. These words were presented to the rater in syntactic categories with the words arranged in alphabetical order (e.g., nouns: baseball, house, river; pronouns: I, them; verbs: hit, run, swam; adjectives: blue, smooth; adverbs: normally, quite). Correlations were then used to compare these predictions to participants' actual self-reported scores.

For both the turn and lexical analyses, we calculated the mean squared error (MSE) as a measure of overall discrepancy between the LLM-predicted and self-reported scores. Specifically, for each participant and trait, we calculated the squared difference between predicted and self-reported trait scores. We then averaged squared errors across traits to generate a single measure of error for each participant, i.e., MSE. This error was then compared across conditions using one-way repeated measures ANOVA.

In Experiment 2, we compared correlations generated from the same individuals-specifically, correlations between self-reported personality and the rater's predicted personality based on chats with the mirror AI or the inverse AI. This analysis used Williams' test for dependent correlations (Steiger, 1980). As in Experiment 1, we used repeated measures ANOVA to compare MSE between conditions and traits.

We used two-tailed Pearson correlations and a Type I error (α) level of .05, adjusting this threshold for multiple comparisons using a Holm-Bonferroni correction. Average correlations across traits were calculated using Fisher z-transformation. Correlations are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

Results

Experiment 1 tested the extent to which personality traits are conveyed in brief text-based interactions with AI. Ninety-nine participants completed the BFI questionnaire, and then had an unstructured chat with the LLM GPT-4.1. These interactions were 26 conversational turns, with participants writing a median of 430 words (range: 134 to 1431). A second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) identified elements in their text that revealed information about their personality. The rater then completed the BFI acting like each participant, mimicking their selections based on its analysis.

Figure 2A shows correlations between the rater's inferred trait scores and participants' self-reported scores for each personality trait. The figure also shows correlations between self-reported trait scores and scores predicted by friends and family (i.e., self-other correlations) drawn from a previous meta-analysis (Connelly & Ones, 2010). For each BFI trait, we observed significant positive correlations between the predicted scores and participants' self-reported scores. The correlations averaged r = .37-comparable in magnitude to reported self-other correlations from friends (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/OiPg/?prefix=M%20%3D%20.35%2C Connelly & Ones, 2010). The highest correlation was observed for Neuroticism (r(97) = .47, 95% CI [.29, .60], p < .001) and the lowest for Conscientiousness (r(97) = .25, 95% CI [.05, .42], p = .013; see Appendix 2). In two cases-Neuroticism and Agreeableness-the correlations were numerically greater than meta-analytic self-other correlations from family. Taken together, this provides evidence for our primary preregistered hypothesis: meaningful personality signals emerge in short, unscripted interactions with LLMs.

Turn Analyses

In a second preregistered analysis, we hypothesized that correlations between predicted and self-reported BFI traits would decrease with less conversational text. To test this, we had the rater generate predictions with 13 and 5 turns from each conversation. Participants produced a median of 204 words (range: 56 to 784) in the 13 turn transcript, and 80 words (range: 18 to 476) in the 5 turn transcript.

Figure 2B shows how correlations between the predicted scores and participants' self-reported scores for each BFI trait changed as the amount of conversation decreased. With less than half the text of the original interaction, we observed significant positive correlations between predicted and self-reported BFI traits for four of the five traits (Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Extraversion, and Openness). Correlations averaged r = .31 (range: .19 to .40). With 5 turns, the rater predicted only two of the five traits (Neuroticism and Openness) better than chance, and the average correlation was r = .20 (range: .09 to .29; see Appendix 2). Across traits, we used one-way repeated measures ANOVA to compare how MSE between predicted and self-reported trait scores changed as the amount of conversation changed. Compared to 26 conversational turns, MSE increased as the number of turns decreased (F(1.56, 152.86) = 31.82, p < .001, ηp² = .25). All pairwise turn comparisons were significant after a correction for multiple comparisons (26 vs 13 turns, t(98) = 3.63, p < .001, dz = .36; 26 vs 5 turns, t(98) = 6.40, p < .001, dz = .64; 13 vs 5 turns, t(98) = 5.42, p < .001, dz = .54). Figure 2D (top panel) depicts these results as the change in MSE as the amount of conversation was reduced from 26 turns to 13 and then 5 turns (see Appendix 2). Thus, the rater's ability to predict BFI traits depended on the amount of conversation, although the rater could predict some traits like Neuroticism with as few as 5 conversational turns.

Linguistic Analyses

A lexical hypothesis of personality proposes that personality traits are represented in language (Allport & Odbert, 1936; Galton, 1884; Goldberg, 1993). Related work found that the words people use often reflect their personality (Yarkoni, 2010). This suggests that the rater's trait predictions might be driven by word choice, with little contribution from conversational context (what the AI said) and syntax. To test this, we assessed the rater's ability to predict participants' BFI traits following the removal of 1) the AI's responses and 2) all filler words and temporal context, providing the rater with only a categorized list of the nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs that participants wrote, alphabetized within each syntactic category.

Figure 2C shows this data.

Excluding the AI's messages had little impact on the correlation between LLM predicted and self-reported BFI traits. All five correlations were significant, averaging r = .36 (range: .20 to .47). When the LLM's predictions were based solely on the content words participants produced, only Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism were predicted at better than chance, and the average correlation fell to r = .27 (range: .19 to .34; see Appendix 2).

Across traits, we used one-way repeated measures ANOVA to compare how MSE between predicted and self-reported trait scores changed as the type of information used in the prediction changed. Providing the rater with the full participant-AI conversation versus what participants wrote versus only the content words and pronouns participants wrote did not reliably change the rater's prediction (F(1.45, 141.85) = 2.16, p = .134, ηp² = .02). Figure 2D (bottom panel) depicts these results as the change in MSE as the type of information was changed (see Appendix 2). With the correlational analyses, this suggests that the words participants used in conversation, as opposed to how they combined them, were the best signals of personality.

Interactions with AI Personalities

Experiment 1 demonstrated that meaningful personality signals can be detected in short, unstructured interactions with AI. In Experiment 2, we tested the extent to which the AI's instructed personality might influence these signals. Using a similar method to Experiment 1, 95 participants completed the BFI, and then had an unstructured chat with two LLMs. One LLM was prompted to mimic participants' self-reported personality traits in language and conversation style, while the other was prompted to mimic the opposite of participants' personality traits. Participants wrote a median of 377 words (range: 131 to 1007) when they spoke with the mirror AI, and 394 words (range: 142 to 1056) when they spoke with the inverse AI. There was no difference in the number of words they produced with each (t(94) = -1.31, p = .19, dz = -.13). Like Experiment 1, the rater was given the transcript from each interaction and instructed to identify elements in the text that revealed information about the participant's personality. The rater then completed the BFI acting like each participant, and we compared these scores with self-report. Figure 3A shows correlations between rater-predicted trait scores and participants' self-reported trait scores. When predictions were based on transcripts of conversations with the mirror AI, correlations with self-reported traits averaged r = .41, with four of five traits predicted better than chance (see Appendix 2). As in Experiment 1, the highest correlation was observed for Neuroticism (r(93) = .63, 95% CI [.49, .74], p < .001) and the lowest for Conscientiousness (r(93) = .14, 95% CI [-.06, .33], p = .17). When predictions were based on conversations with the inverse AI, correlations averaged r = .30 (range: .15 to .44), with only three of five traits predicted better than chance. The rater's ability to predict Neuroticism was significantly better when the prediction was based on conversations with the LLM that mirrored participants' personality (r = .63 vs r = .18: t(92) = 6.50, p < .001). Importantly, this pattern of results was similar when the rater's predictions were based only on the messages participants sent, rather than on the entire conversation (see Appendix 2).

Next, we compared differences in MSE from self-report between predictions based on conversations with the mirror AI, and predictions based on conversations with the inverse AI. There was an interaction between LLM personality (mirror versus inverse) and error associated with each trait (F(3.20, 300.8) = 7.84, p < .001, ηp² = .08). The rater predicted Neuroticism with more error when the prediction was based on chats with the inverse AI compared to the mirror AI (t(94) = 4.86, p < .001, dz = .50). Figure 3B shows differences in MSE between predictions from inverse and mirror conversations (see Appendix 2).

As in Experiment 1 (Figure 2C), we examined the extent to which the rater's prediction was based on the words participants chose to use as opposed to conversational context and syntax. Participants produced a median of 243 (range: 87 to 684) content words and pronouns with the mirror AI, and 262 (range: 97 to 720) content words and pronouns with the inverse AI. There was no difference in the number of these words participants wrote with each (t(94) = -1.15, p = .25, dz = -.12).

Figure 3C shows correlations between the rater's predicted BFI trait scores and participants' self-reported scores when the rater's prediction was based solely on the content words and pronouns participants wrote.

For words shared with the mirror AI, these correlations averaged r = .40 (range: .21 to .60) and all five traits were predicted better than chance. None of the correlations were significant when they were based on words shared with the inverse AI (average r = .03, range: -.25 to .15). For three of five traits, we observed a statistical difference between predictions using words shared with the mirror AI and those shared with the inverse AI-Neuroticism (r = .60 vs r = -.25: t(92) = 8.49, p < .001), Extraversion (r = .44 vs r = .04: t(92) = 3.78, p < .01), and Openness (r = .45 vs r = .15: t(92) = 2.96, p < .05). This dissociation was also reflected in the MSE from self-reported traits associated with the predictions (interaction between LLM personality and error for each trait prediction: F(2.93, 275.4) = 12.03, p < .001, ηp² = .11). For every trait, predictions had less error when they were based on words used with the mirror AI (Figure 3D; see Appendix 2).

Finally, we explored whether the differences in Experiment 2 might reflect mimicry of the AI's language, rather than participants' own word choice. To test this, we applied a conservative filter, removing content words produced by participants that were repetitions of lemmas (dictionary headwords) written by the AI in previous messages. For example, if the AI used the words go and run, all variants used by the participant in later messages (e.g., running, ran, went, gone) were removed. We then had the rater predict participants' traits based on the content words and pronouns that remained. Although this strict approach likely removed words that genuinely reflected self-expression, it also controlled for mimicry.

Applying this filter left a median of 180 participant words (range: 65 to 540) with the mirror AI and 197 participant words (range: 54 to 543) with the inverse AI, with no statistical difference in word counts between these conditions (t(94) = -1.51, p = .14, dz = -.16). Even with this restricted text, the rater predicted three of five traits in the case of words written to the mirror AI (Neuroticism, Openness, and Extraversion), and no traits in the case of the inverse AI. A statistical difference was still observed for predictions of Neuroticism between the mirror and inverse conditions (r = .49 vs r = -.07: t(92) = 5.26, p < .001). More generally, the pattern of correlations and MSE between rater-predicted and self-reported traits looked similar to that observed with all content words included (see Figure S1 and Tables S1-2). Thus, the extent to which participants conveyed some traits solely through words they had not seen the AI produce depended on whether the AI's persona mirrored their personality.

Discussion

We tested the extent to which unconstrained, text-based conversations with AI convey personality traits. Participants had conversations with the LLM GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. A second LLM then predicted participants' Big Five personality traits based on the text of the conversations. Correlations with self-reported traits were positive and significant in each case. As hypothesized, the rater's ability to predict personality decreased as the amount of conversation it had access to decreased. But even with only half the conversation, four out of five personality traits were predicted at better than chance. A linguistic analysis revealed that in conversations with AI people conveyed their personality through word choice, with syntax and conversational context playing a smaller role. In a second study, we applied Experiment 1's method to data involving conversations with AI that either mirrored or opposed participants' personalities. In this case, linguistic signals of personality were especially strong in conversations when the AI's persona mirrored participants' personalities.

How Meaningful Were the LLM Predictions?

Unlike traits such as height and eye colour, personality isn't a static property of people-it's primarily measured using self-report and these measurements reflect the social and psychological context in which they occurred. In reflection of this, the test-retest reliability of personality questionnaires like the BFI or other inventories ranges from .7 to .8 (Gnambs, 2014; John & Srivastava, 1999; McCrae et al., 2011)-lower than other psychological traits such as IQ (https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/vXoX. Brown & May, 1979). How meaningful is a personality prediction that correlates with self-report at r = .37? Comparisons with similar personality predictions made by friends and family help contextualize the predictions observed here. Using meta-analysis, Connelly and Ones (2010) report that, across traits, predictions of personality made by friends (defined as people with a mutual liking who have known each other for a median of 3 years) correlate with self-report at .35. In the case of family (defined as people linked by genetics or marriage who have known each other for a median of 17 years) the same correlation was .43. The predictions generated here from short conversations with AI align with these values, and, for some traits, numerically exceed them. Thus, the predictions were meaningful in the sense that they were as good as predictions made by people who know each other well, in some cases, extraordinarily so (e.g., spouses and family members).

Syntax as an Expression of Personality Conversation requires the selection of words and their arrangement. To what extent does syntax convey personality in conversation?

In Experiment 1, predictions of personality from conversations with AI were similar between predictions made using the full conversations and predictions that relied solely on the content words and pronouns that participants shared. This was also observed in Experiment 2, but only when the AI's personality mirrored participants' personality. When the AI's personality opposed participants' personality, three significant trait predictions collapsed when only the participants' content words and pronouns were considered. In this case, syntax may have helped the rater avoid confusing displays of empathy with words that signaled personality. The words in the sentence, I'm sorry you're feeling depressed, for example, could be confused as a signal of depression when viewed as an alphabetized list of content words and pronouns (Pham et al., 2021). Thus, how people combine words can convey meaningful signals of personality in some circumstances.

Neuroticism Was Strongly Conveyed

People readily convey personality in short conversations with AI, but they don't convey all traits equally. Here, Neuroticism was the strongest signal. In Experiment 1, the correlation between predictions of this trait and self-report was .47; in Experiment 2, when the AI's prompted personality mirrored participants, it was .63. This is potentially problematic. Neuroticism is associated with anxiety and depression (Kotov et al.https://paperpile.com/c/lE3KgO/ophN+HC3B 2010; Malouff et al., 2005) , and, as noted, LLMs converge their output towards the word choice and linguistic style of conversational partners (Blevins, 2026; P. Chen et al., 2026). Future work should test the extent to which LLM mimicry of Neuroticism might exacerbate disorders of mental health. Critically, Experiment 2 also demonstrated that when the AI exhibited an opposite personality to participants, linguistic signatures of Neuroticism collapsed. One safeguard against the reinforcement of negative psychological traits by AI might be through the regulation of the personas AI are instructed to mimic.

LLMs as Psychometric Tools

What role do LLMs play in psychological measurement? There's a longstanding tension in psychology between self-report measures of psychological variables and more implicit measurements from computer-based tasks (Corneille & Gawronski, 2024; Moreau, 2025; Zimmerman, 2024). Computerized behavioural tasks quantify psychological traits by fitting formal computational models developed from neurocognitive theory to raw behavioural data (Corlett & Fletcher, 2014; Montague et al., 2012; Wilson & Collins, 2019)-a tradition echoing behaviourism's rejection of introspection (Watson, 1913). Psychometricians counter that implicit measures lack crucial properties of validated self-report questionnaires, like test-retest reliability, efficiency of administration, and predictive validity for real-world outcomes (Corneille & Gawronski, 2024). LLMs offer a method to bridge self-report with more implicit measures of psychology (Wright et al., 2026). Conversation is one of the most common human behaviours. By applying psychometric principles to the text of raw, unconstrained conversations-which can be less susceptible to the social desirability biases that shape self-report (Paulhus, 1984; Vazire, 2010)-LLMs can reproduce self-report psychometric scores directly from natural language. For example, Suthaharan et al. (2026) used an LLM to rate metacognition from free-text descriptions after a behavioural task, and LLM-inferred metacognition moderated task performance. In combination with the current study and related work, this provides evidence that LLMs can be used to combine the psychometric rigour of self-report with the naturalism of human behaviour.

Limitations

Although our findings demonstrate that an LLM can infer personality traits from the language people chose to share in conversations with AI, the extent to which AI can glean personality from human-to-human conversations is unclear. When people are asked to rate the personality of others following short interactions, their predictions weakly correlate with self-report (Wall et al., 2013). People may reveal more about their personality traits in conversations with AI, as these conversations might feel less observed and AI systems are good at mimicking empathy. For example, Lucas et al., (2014) demonstrated that participants were willing to disclose more personal information to a virtual human when they believed it was being controlled by a computer versus a person. Third party raters perceived AI responses as more compassionate than human responses, even when they knew the response was AI-generated (Ovsyannikova et al., 2025). But other evidence is more mixed. Croes et al. (2024) found no difference in participants' self-rated intimacy of disclosures between disclosures to chatbots and humans, but there was less fear of judgement when disclosing to a chatbot. The extent to which people share their psychology through word choice with LLMs versus other people has yet to be directly tested. This paper presents a framework for pursuing this work.

Conclusions

In a preregistered study, we demonstrated that human personality is expressed through short, unstructured interactions with AI. Participants conveyed personality largely through word choice, and this was especially true when the LLM's personality mirrored participants. These personality signals were meaningful, matching self-other predictions from friends and, in some cases, family. Some traits like Neuroticism could be identified with only a few hundred words of conversation. Thus, signals of personality are recoverable from short, unstructured conversations with AI. Given the extent to which humans now engage with LLMs, people may be sharing more about their psychology with AI systems than they realize.
